o: Byla to běžná policejní událost: ve čtyři hodiny ráno přejelo auto v Žitné ulici opilou stařenu a v největší rychlosti ujelo.
t: It was an ordinary police case: at four in the morning a car ran over a drunken old woman in Žitná Street and sped off at top speed.

t: "Oh, good Lord," dr. Mejzlík lamented, "how am I supposed to find out which car it was then?

t: Please, he's waiting next door."

t: "Then bring him in," said Dr. Mejzlík disgustedly, vainly trying to work something out of the meagre report. "Please, name and address," he said mechanically; he didn't even look at the witness.

o: “Králík Jan, studující strojního inženýrství,” pronesl svědek pevně.
t: "Jan Králík, a student of mechanical engineering," the witness stated firmly.

t: "So you were there, sir, when an unknown car ran over Božena Macháčková at four o'clock this morning."

t: "Jaroslav Nerad, a poet," said the witness with a certain pride. "But he probably wouldn't tell you anything either."

t: "A four-cylinder explosive engine," said the expert witness. "I don't know much about car makes, though."

t: "I don't know," said the bewildered witness. "I think it was some sort of black car; but I didn't look closely, because when the accident happened, I said to Nerad: Look, those rascals will run a man down and not even stop!"

o: “Hm,” mínil dr. Mejzlík nespokojeně, “to je sice docela místná a správná morální reakce, ale já bych byl raději, kdybyste si všiml čísla vozu.
t: "Hm," Dr. Mejzlík said unhappily, "that's a rather local and correct moral reaction, but I would have preferred it if you had noticed the car's number.

o: To je úžasné, pane, jak lidé nedovedou pozorovat.
t: It's amazing, sir, how people are unable to observe.

o: Vy ovšem víte, že šofér je vinen, vy ovšem správně soudíte, že ti lidé jsou lotři, ale na číslo se nekouknete.
t: You do know, of course, that the driver is at fault; you do judge correctly that those men are rascals, but you don't look at the number.

o: Soudit dovede každý; ale pořádně, věcně si všimnout věcí - Děkuju vám, pane Králíku; nebudu vás zdržovat.”
t: Anyone can judge; but to observe things properly, factually—Thank you, Mr. Králík; I won't keep you."

o: Za hodinu zazvonil strážník číslo 141 u bytné básníka Jaroslava Nerada.
t: An hour later, policeman number 141 rang the bell at the apartment of the poet Jaroslav Nerad.

t: Yes, the poet is at home, but he's asleep.

o: Básník vykulil ze dveří malá užaslá očka na strážníka; nemohl se jaksi upamatovat, co vlastně provedl.
t: The poet goggled small, astounded eyes at the policeman from the doorway; he somehow couldn't recall what he had actually done.

o: Nakonec přece jenom pochopil, proč má jít na policii. “Musí to být?” ptal se nedůvěřivě. “Já se totiž na nic už nepamatuju; já byl v noci trochu -“
t: In the end he did understand why he was going to the police. "Must I?" he asked mistrustfully. "I don't remember anything anymore; I was a little—"

o: “- nalitej,” děl strážník chápavě. “Pane, já jsem poznal mnoho básníků.
t: "—tipsy," said the policeman comprehendingly. "Sir, I've known many poets.

o: Tak se, pane, ustrojte; mám na vás počkat?”
t: So, sir, get yourself ready; shall I wait for you?"

o: Načež se básník a strážník dostali do řeči o nočních lokálech, o životě vůbec, o zvláštních úkazech na nebi a mnohých jiných předmětech; jen politika byla oběma cizí.
t: Thereupon the poet and the policeman fell to talking about night trains, about life in general, about strange phenomena in the sky and many other things; only politics was alien to both of them.

o: Takto v přátelském a poučném hovoru se dostal básník na policii.
t: Thus, in a friendly and instructive conversation, the poet arrived at the police station.

o: “Vy jste pan Nerad Jaroslav, básník,” řekl mu dr. Mejzlík. “Pane svědku, vy jste byl při tom, když neznámé auto přejelo Boženu Macháčkovou.”
t: "You are Mr. Nerad Jaroslav, the poet," Dr. Mejzlík said to him. "Mr. Witness, you were present when an unknown car ran over Božena Macháčková."

o: Básník usilovně přemýšlel. “To nevím,” řekl, “já jsem si toho nevšiml.”
t: The poet thought hard. "I don't know," he said, "I didn't notice it."

o: “Nevzpomínáte si na žádnou podrobnost?” naléhal Mejzlík.
t: "You don't remember a single detail?" Mejzlík pressed.

t: "Not at all," the poet said honestly. "You see, I don't pay attention to details."

o: “Tak prosím vás,” spustil dr. Mejzlík ironicky, “co jste tedy vůbec pozoroval?”
t: "So please," Dr. Mejzlík began ironically, "what did you actually notice?"

o: “Tu celou náladu,” pravil básník neurčitě. “Víte, tu opuštěnou ulici… takovou dlouhou… za úsvitu… a jak tam ta ženská zůstala ležet -” Najednou vyskočil. “Vždyť já jsem o tom něco napsal, když jsem přišel domů!”
t: "The whole mood," the poet said vaguely. "You know, that deserted street… so long… at daybreak… and how the woman stayed lying there—" Suddenly he sprang up. "But I did write something about it when I got home!"

o: Hrabal se ve všech kapsách a vytahal množství obálek, účtů a jiných takových hadrů. “Ne, tohle to není,” brumlal, “tohle taky ne - Počkejme, snad je to tohle,” mínil pohřížen v pozorování rubu jakési obálky.
t: He rummaged through all his pockets, pulling out envelopes, receipts and other such junk. "No, that's not it," he muttered, "this isn't it either— Wait a moment, maybe it's this," he said, squinting at the fabric of some envelope.

t: "It's nothing," the poet objected. "But if you like, I'll read it to you."

t: “I don't think so,” Dr. Mejzlík said critically. “For my part, I cannot make out how that on the fifteenth of July, at four in the morning in Žitná Street, a car ran over Božena Macháčková, a sixty-year-old drunken woman; she was taken away wounded to the General Hospital and is fighting for her life.

t: "Let me see," said the poet, baffled, and leaned over the paper. "'A swan's neck, breasts, a drum and cymbals' - what is that supposed to be?"

t: "Wait," the poet pondered, "something must have been there that reminded me - Listen, doesn't a two sometimes look like a swan's neck to you?

t: "Wait," said Dr. Mejzlík and wrote 235 on a scrap of paper. "Are you sure that car had the number 235?"

o: “Já jsem si vůbec žádného čísla nevšiml,” prohlásil Jaroslav Nerad rozhodně. “Ale něco takového tam muselo být - kdepak by se to tu vzalo?” divil se, hloubaje nad básnickou. “Ale víte, to místo je to nejlepší z celé básně.”
t: "I didn't notice any number at all," Jaroslav Nerad declared firmly. "But something like that must have been there—where else would it come from?" he wondered, brooding over the poem. "But you know, that place is the best in the whole poem."

o: Za dva dny navštívil dr. Mejzlík básníka; básník tentokrát nespal, nýbrž měl tam nějakou dívku a marně sháněl prázdnou židli, aby ji policejnímu úředníkovi nabídl.
t: Two days later Dr. Mejzlík visited the poet; this time the poet wasn't asleep, but had some girl there and was vainly hunting for an empty chair to offer the police official.

o: “Já už zase běžím,” řekl dr. Mejzlík. “Já vám jen jdu říci, že to byl opravdu vůz číslo 235.”
t: "I'm off again," said Dr. Mejzlík. "I only came to tell you that it really was car number 235."

o: “Jaký vůz?” užasl básník.
